note.label: Much Is Given, Much Is Required

precepts.why:
“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted.” He has chosen and set apart every man here, all the captains, to preach good tidings to the meek. But how do you bind up a person that is broken? The brokenhearted are broken in the mind: suffering the curses without knowing the will of God. We are set apart to bind them up. What do we bind them with?

“Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples.” We bind up the testimony and seal the law in the minds of the people, because they are brokenhearted and their minds are broken. That is what we are called to do: to bind them to the laws of God.

And we show them why it is good. Look at our lives as the example of what it means to serve God and why it is good to serve him. That means we have to be sincere about it. How do we tell the people to touch not the unclean thing and then not live it ourselves? The one who was profitable to many but not to himself will be punished accordingly, because he knew better.

So the good tidings we proclaim with the law are these: if we repent and keep God's laws in sincerity and endure to the end, he will deliver us, and we will rule again, as we were made in his image to rule.

note.label: Much Is Given, Much Is Required

precepts.why:
Isaiah 61 says to “proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord”, and Isaiah 49 says it again: “Thus saith the Lord, In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages.” The acceptable year and the acceptable time: that is when we heal the broken heart and proclaim liberty to the captives.

“The Lord hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name. And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me; And said unto me, Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified.” We are supposed to glorify our God in this body.

“Then I said, I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought, and in vain: yet surely my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.” We go to stiff-necked, hard-hearted people who refuse to hear the word of God, but we still proclaim the day of the Lord to heal those minds and tell them there is an end to this: we will rule one day. He formed us from the womb “to bring Jacob again to him.”

“It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel.” It may not appear that we are doing it, but when the numbers come in, it is a light thing he has given us, and he still charges us to raise up the children of Israel. “I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth”: that goes back to Matthew 4, the Gentiles of Galilee. Our job is to bring salvation to the people and lead them back to him, and that is a great ministry.

“Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship” … “and he shall choose thee.” Out of all of them, he is going to choose us. And unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: we want to be the faithful servant the Lord finds doing this work in sincerity, without deceit and without secret sins.

note.label: The Kingdom Of Adam And The Old World

precepts.why:
2 Esdras 3:6 says God led Adam “into paradise, which thy right hand had planted”, and Genesis 2:8 says the same thing: “the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.” Adam's kingdom ruled the heaven and the earth. The man who could go to paradise, where the Lord is, did not walk around without clothes. Then verse 9: “And out of the ground made the Lord God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food”. What is that talking about?

Isaiah 61:3: “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord”. The trees of righteousness are Israel: us, in paradise, in our heavenly bodies.

Reading Genesis 2:9 again: the trees pleasant to the sight and good for food are a similitude for Adam's sons in the heavens, the righteous. “the tree of life also in the midst of the garden”: the twelve apostles were up there, the 144 were there, all twelve tribes were there. “and the tree of knowledge of good and evil”: that is Satan. The tree people set up and worship in their houses at Christmas references that tree; Babylon referenced it, and Santa Claus is Satan Claus.

God works hand in hand with the prophets. He has Moses write something hard, and he has the other prophets come and explain what it is talking about. Isaiah explains the trees of Genesis: the planting of the Lord is his people.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
Isaiah 61 is fulfilled in Christ, who read it himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor.” The good tidings of Isaiah are the gospel. And the poor are not everybody: “the Lord hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it.” The poor are the poor of Zion. You do not even have to go to Isaiah 14; Isaiah 61 itself says it is them that mourn in Zion.

“he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives.” We are the captives. How can you read captive and think everybody? Rome was dominating Israel at that time. “and recovering of sight to the blind”: we are the blind people. “to set at liberty them that are bruised”: bruised in sin.

“To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.” The acceptable year of the Lord is our day of jubilee, and we had better accept that.

Imagine the Israelites and the Romans sitting in church together, the captives and the captors side by side, told we are all the same. It makes no sense. Jake looks over at Esau to see if he is upset, and if master is upset at this reading, he disregards it: black Christians hate anything that upsets white folks, and that is why they do not believe. But Christ read it plainly: he came to proclaim liberty to the captives of Israel, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound, bound in these prisons we call America, the Caribbean and whatever lands we are in.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
“the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek.” Christ read it in Luke 4 as “to preach the gospel to the poor.” When it says the poor, who is that? Isaiah answers: “What shall one then answer the messengers of the nation? That the Lord hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it.”

That is telling you who the poor are: the poor of Zion, the poor of his people. Zion is another name for the Israelites.

And Isaiah 61 itself agrees: he came “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes”. Why are we mourning? Because we are captive.

So the good tidings, the brokenhearted, the captives and them that are bound are not all nations. They are the poor of the Lord’s people, the Israelites in captivity, who shall trust in the Zion the Lord has founded.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
When the captives are set free, “ye shall be named the Priests of the Lord”, “For your shame ye shall have double”, and “their seed shall be known among the Gentiles, and their offspring among the people: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed which the Lord hath blessed.” No matter where we go on this planet they are going to know our children by name. Today you want to talk to your boss and he turns his back to you; on that day they are going to beg for your attention.

Zephaniah is the precept to that: “Behold, at that time I will undo all that afflict thee.” He is going to undo all the nations that afflict us. “and I will save her that halteth”: we are the ones that halt, because we are captive. “and gather her that was driven out.”

“and I will get them praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame.” We get that fame and that glory, and our children are going to get it too. Everybody is going to acknowledge who we are. “At that time will I bring you again, even in the time that I gather you: for I will make you a name and a praise among all people of the earth, when I turn back your captivity before your eyes, saith the Lord.”

That is the liberty proclaimed to the captives in Isaiah 61: not only freed, but honoured in the very lands that shamed us.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
Isaiah 61 proclaims “the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God.” There is a particular day in a particular year when God will come to deliver his people. Isaiah 63 shows that day: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength?” This is Christ, the Son of God, and his garment is glorious, not a sheet or a robe.

“Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat?” Isaiah is asking Christ, Why are you red? It looks like you were stomping grapes. “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me.” Christ trod down the nations and killed them alone. He did not need the help of the twelve tribes of Israel; he did it himself.

“for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments.” The wine represents their blood.

“For the day of vengeance is in mine heart, and the year of my redeemed is come.” We are the redeemed. The year of my redeemed is the acceptable year of the Lord in Isaiah 61, our jubilee, and it comes with the day of vengeance on the nations.

note.label: Genesis 3: The Craftiness of Your Enemy

precepts.why:
“he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness”. The Most High clothes His saints with righteousness; He covers them.

That is what the coats of skins were about. When the Lord God made “coats of skins, and clothed them”, it was a covering for sin: animal sacrifice to cover the sins of Adam and his wife. As Adam was clothed to cover sin, the saints are clothed and covered with righteousness.

note.label: Numbers 23: How Shall I Curse, Whom God Hath Not Cursed?

precepts.why:
The last end of Israel that Balaam wished to share: “For your shame ye shall have double; and for confusion they shall rejoice in their portion: therefore in their land they shall possess the double: everlasting joy shall be unto them.” Double for our shame, and everlasting joy.

“For I the Lord love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them.” An everlasting covenant, and a seed the nations will know: “And their seed shall be known among the Gentiles, and their offspring among the people: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed which the Lord hath blessed.”

The people that shall not be reckoned among the nations will be acknowledged by all that see them as the seed which the Lord hath blessed. That is why we cannot wait for those days.

We are blessed of the Lord which made heaven and earth, and we will bless the Lord from this time forth and for evermore.

note.label: Isaiah 61: The Spirit of the Lord God Is Upon Me

precepts.why:
“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound”. Christ quoted this passage when he read in the synagogue: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised”.

He applied the anointing to preach the gospel to himself. The anointed one of Isaiah 61, sent to the meek and the brokenhearted, to the captives and them that are bound, is Christ. He is the one sent to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance of our God, to comfort all that mourn, and to give beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning and the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness, that they might be called trees of righteousness.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

precepts.why:
“(Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.)” Moses was the meekest man in all Israel. He submitted to God's will 100%. Here the term humble is often translated as meek, highlighting Moses' exemplary character in leading the Israelites with patience and reliance on God.

That is what meek means in Isaiah 61: humility, gentleness, and submission to God's will. Not soft. Meekness is strength under control, God's control. We all must be meek.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

precepts.why:
“But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.” The reward for meekness: those who are gentle and humble, who submit themselves to God's will, receive God's blessings and inherit the land.

The good tidings of Isaiah 61 are preached to these meek.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

precepts.why:
“Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.” So, blessed are the meek, those that submit themselves to God's will. Part of the Beatitudes, this statement by Christ underscores the value of meekness in the kingdom of heaven, promising eternal inheritance to those who embody this virtue.

Back to Isaiah 61:1: to preach the gospel, good tidings, unto the meek. The meek, as we just looked up, means those who submit to God's will.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

precepts.why:
“For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them,” So Christ will feed us. “and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters: and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.” All tears.

So these Israelites, our people, we would be in a constant state of being brokenhearted. That's why it says God is the one who shall wipe away all our tears from our eyes.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

precepts.why:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.” There shall be no more death. Neither sorrow. Nor crying. Neither shall there be any more pain.

Former things like what? Oppression, captivity, poverty. All that's going to be done away with. So he's going to wipe away all our tears from our eyes: that is how he binds up the brokenhearted.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

precepts.why:
Liberty to the captives, because Christ spoke on that. “And they shall fall by the edge of the sword,” The Israelites shall fall by the edge of Rome's sword. “and shall be led away captive into all nations:” Highlight that word captive. Into all nations. “and Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled.”

So that didn't just stop at 70 AD. That curse continued after Rome: you had Spain, France, Britain, America. It continued, being led away captive into all nations.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

precepts.why:
Still dealing with liberty to the captives. “If they sin against thee, (for there is no man that sinneth not,) and thou be angry with them,” And God was angry with us. “and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them away captives unto the land of the enemy, far or near;” Delivered us to who? To the enemy. Where? Unto the land of the enemy, like the United States of America.

“Yet if they shall bethink themselves in the land whither they were carried captives, and repent, and make supplication unto thee in the land of them that carried them captives, saying, We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have committed wickedness;” So King Solomon was prophesying that the Israelites would be carried away captive, and if we wanted deliverance from captivity we would have to bethink ourselves: remember who we are as a people, remember that we are the twelve tribes of Israel. We would also have to repent and make great supplication to the Lord and confess with our mouth, we have sinned, we have done perversely, we have committed wickedness. Meek means humility, gentleness, and submission to God's will. Like another scripture says, Moses was the meekest man in all Israel: he submitted to God's will 100%. We all must be meek. Meek don't mean you be soft and listen to some idiot on the street. No. It is often associated with a spirit of patience and a lack of self-assertiveness, and that ain't right; that's how most people think of it. Meekness is not to be confused with weakness. Rather, it is strength under control. Whose control? God's control. It involves a conscious choice to put others before oneself and to trust in God's sovereignty and justice. So the meek are those brothers and sisters who 100% submit themselves to the will of God.

“he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted,” Pause on brokenhearted. In the Bible, being brokenhearted means a state of deep grief, spiritual bankruptcy, and crushed spirit. You don't get no more spiritually bankrupt than black people. Recognizing one's need for God, leading to humility and repentance, where God promises to be near, heal, and restore those in this condition; often described as a shattered, wounded inner self ready for divine intervention. Emotional and spiritual ruin: intense emotional pain, despair, loss, or feeling spiritually crushed and helpless, like something shattered or torn apart. You don't get no more brokenhearted than our people. That's what slavery was about. We are a race of brokenhearted men and women. Everybody on the planet ain't brokenhearted; the social elite are not brokenhearted. Brokenhearted is our race, our people, us on the street crying for reparations. That's a broken heart right there. They said, "Pull yourself up by your bootstraps," but we can't even afford boots sometimes. In fact, not that we can't afford boots: you stole our boots. The brokenhearted is our race because we are the ones who've gone through the harshest and worst captivity, the most cruel captivity, where we even lost our language, heritage, our identity. No other people went through that.

“to proclaim liberty to the captives,” Now, if you read liberty to the captives and say that's everybody, there's something wrong with you. We're the captive race. We're the ones that were brought here against our will, shackled and chained and kept here. The hell is wrong with people talking about, "Oh no, the gospel is for everybody"? It's telling you liberty to the captives. Maybe you don't know what captive means: captive, one taken in war. Captives were often treated with great cruelty and indignity. When a city was taken by assault, all the men were slain and the women and children carried away captive and sold as slaves. How you going to read the gospel is for the captives and go, "No, the gospel is for everybody"? Everybody didn't go into captivity. You'll be on the street teaching and there's always a dumb Christian who says everybody went into slavery, all nations at one time or another went into slavery. That's a lie. When did the Chinese go into slavery? Don't tell me about the indentured servitude they were brought over here under; they got paid. Don't tell me about the East Indians that were brought over here; that's indentured servitude, that's not slavery, that's not being captive. And when did Netanyahu and his people go into slavery? World War II is not slavery. Captives were sometimes carried away into foreign countries. Is this not a foreign country? As was the case with the Jews. Boom. We are the ones that are still captive today.

“and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;” Prison: in biblical times the concept of prison and imprisonment appears in various contexts reflecting both physical and spiritual dimensions. Physical and spiritual. Christians think everything is just spiritual. No. Everything ain't just spiritual. Prisons were used as places of confinement for those awaiting trial or punishment. We are a brokenhearted and destitute people: look at the ghettos. That's become normal. That's a prison for our people, but it's so normal that that's home. Look at the war that's going on there. Our people see it as normal, and when you see your oppression as normal there's something psychologically wrong; you've been broken in your mind. Prisons also serve as powerful metaphors for spiritual bondage and deliverance, and that's how Christians use it; they keep everything right there. In the Old Testament prisons were often simple structures or even pits where individuals were detained; one of the earliest mentions is Joseph, imprisoned in Egypt.

Bound: the concept of being bound in the Bible carries both literal and metaphorical meanings, often signifying physical restraint, spiritual bondage or covenantal obligations. So it's literal and spiritual. Physical restraint, we know what that one is. Why get into the spiritual bondage now? Because the chains are off of us, and a lot of our people, if you got a good job and you make decent money, you'll be the first ones to say, "I'm not in bondage. I'm not captive. Bro, you wrong." Metaphorically, being bound can refer to spiritual bondage or the enslavement of sin; Jesus speaks of this in John 8:34. So when Christ says the truth shall make you free he's talking about two things: a literal meaning and a spiritual meaning.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

points: “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;” You know what's heavy about that? He said the good tidings, the good news, is for the meek, and those meek are those who are brokenhearted, those who are captive, those who are in prison houses and bound. Then he says in verse 2, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, meaning there is a particular year coming. Then it says the day: there's a particular day coming of vengeance. Vengeance of our God. Vengeance for what? For what we just read in verse 1. And this is what Christians can't see. So that's good news to us: God's coming to kill people to save our race. You can clap to the Lord for that thing. Y'all nervous? Hell yeah.

Vengeance: in the biblical context it refers to the act of retribution or punishment inflicted in response to wrongdoing, a theme throughout the scriptures reflecting both divine justice and human response to injustice. We always crying for justice and we never get it. Ask Rasheem Carter's mama. Ask Sonya Massey's mama. Kendrick Johnson. The concept of vengeance is closely tied to God's holiness and justice as well as the moral order he has established. The Bible frequently speaks of vengeance as belonging to God alone, Deuteronomy 32:35; see, that's why everything in these commentaries is not always right. Real Christians say vengeance is the Lord's, I will repay, saith the Lord. That's true; vengeance does start with the Lord. But once Christ smashes through the armies of this world, watch what he's going to say to us in Ezekiel 25:14. Christians don't want to hear this, but this is what the Bible says.

So there is a particular day coming that the leaders of society are aware of. Christians ignore it; they think there's going to be peace on earth, goodwill toward men all the time. No. The day of vengeance is coming: vengeance for what these nations did to our people, our twelve tribes.

Mourn: mourning in the biblical context refers to the expression of deep sorrow or grief, often associated with death, loss or repentance, a significant theme throughout the scriptures reflecting both personal and communal experiences of lamentation. Lamentations 3 gives the example of what it means to mourn: Jeremiah could not stop crying when he saw the destruction of his black people, and he had to wait for the Lord. That's what we got to do. We can't jump up and do something. When we see these images it hurts inside, it makes some of us cry, but we know we can't do nothing; we have to wait for the Lord to make his return. Before we get to Zion we are a weeping people, always going through some hardship, and God's comfort is that sorrow and mourning shall flee away when we return to the land.

note.label: The Gospel Is Black Liberation

points: Verse 3 really sums it up: who the gospel is for. “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion,” In where? In Zion. Zion is another name for the twelve tribes of Israel. So the good news, the gospel, is not for everybody on the planet. They've been lying since day one.

“to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he might be glorified.” That he might be glorified. So those lamentations, these cries, the mourning that we go through: Sonya Massey, Rasheem Carter, and Trey Reed. Trey Reed is the brother that was hung, and they said he committed suicide; Colin Kaepernick did an independent autopsy and they found the back of his skull was crushed in. So it was not a suicide. They were lying, once again, like with Rasheem Carter, where they said animals cut his skull open perfectly. The lies. And our sister Sonya Massey, 5'1", 130 pounds: "I rebuke you in the name of Jesus," and the guy that's 6 foot 3, an Edomite, shoots her in the face. And then you had people like Officer Tatum and others talking about the cops didn't do nothing wrong. And black Christians say nothing. They turn a blind eye and say absolutely nothing about these atrocities that have been happening for however long.

Look at the names. This is why we mourn in Zion. This is why the glad tidings, the good tidings, is for us, our people. To bind up the brokenhearted: this is why we're brokenhearted. To proclaim liberty to the captives: this is captivity here, but it's become so normal to some of us that we accept this. The opening of the prison to them that are bound, to appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to comfort all that mourn. Ninety percent of these never make the news; some of these names we don't even recognize. So this ain't happening to everybody on the planet.

And one of the things we rarely talk about are black political prisoners: brothers, and some sisters, who were imprisoned back in the 60s fighting for the rights of black and brown people, and their names have virtually been forgotten. They say, "Oh no, but they killed somebody." Well, what was the cop doing? Remember the MOVE movement in 1985, where they dropped C4 on them, shot up and killed those little children, and then lied and said, "Oh no, they were shooting first." That was a lie, and the news proved it was a lie. They did the same thing with Fred Hampton. And our people will see our brothers like this and forget about them. The rights that many of us have today to run our black gums is because of these brothers and sisters that are still incarcerated to this day, and they die in prison, and black Christians who always run their black gums don't give a damn. Black political prisoners are often black activists from movements like the Black Panther Party or Black Liberation Army, unjustly incarcerated for their political beliefs, activities, or race rather than purely criminal acts: Mumia Abu-Jamal, Assata Shakur, Sundiata Acoli and Jalil Muntaqim, many serving decades for actions tied to black liberation struggles.
